questions.question: Explain the operation of a magnetic compass.
questions.idealAnswer: A magnetic compass has two permanent magnets that are free to move. They naturally align themselves with earths magnetic field. An indicating lubber line attached to the magnets displays direction on a graduated dial which allows 360 degrees of movement and indication. The magnets are influenced by the earths magnetic poles and point to the direction as indicated. The compass can be influenced by other magnetic fields, therefor, precautions must be taken during flight deck installations to guard the compass from these influences that cause deviation. Dip error occurs when flying too close to the poles.

questions.question: Explain the basic procedure of swinging a compass.
questions.idealAnswer: A compass rose is usually located somewhere on the surface of the airport. Make sure there is no electromagnetic interference. The aircraft should be placed in normal flight attitude with normal equipment and engines operating. Align the aircraft with the compass rose facing north (0 or 360 degrees) Use a nonferrous screwdriver to make adjustments to the compass. Rotate the adjusting screw so that the indication is 0 degrees or 360 degrees. Then position the aircraft so that is aligned east with the compass rose. Rotate the adjusting screw so that the compass indicates 90 degrees. Reposition the aircraft on the compass rose so that it faces south if the compass reads 180 no further adjustments need to be made.

questions.question: Explain the purpose and operation of a gyroscopic instrument.
questions.idealAnswer: Most gyroscopic instruments are used for direction or attitude indication. They can be driven by air pressure, vacuum, or electricity since the spinning armature of a motor can act as a gyroscope. When rotating a gyroscope it maintains rigidity in space. That is, it will continue to rotate in the same plan of rotation no matter which way its mounting gimbals are moved. This is the basis of a directional gyro. The directional gyro, or DG is commonly relied upon more than the magnetic compass to indicate direction in an aircraft. The gyro spins in the vertical plane and stays aligned with the direction to which it is set. The instrument case and the aircraft move around the ridged gyro. This causes a vertical compass card geared to the rotor gimble to rotate. Typically, a small, fixed airplane in front of the moving card indicates the direction in degrees.

questions.question: How does a pitot and static system operate?
questions.idealAnswer: A pitot system captures air pressure as the aircraft moves forward through the air. Air travels through the pitot tube and the air pressure is converted to an airspeed indicator, and to the digital air date computer (if in use). The pressure is used to calculate and display airspeed. The static system is designed to sense ambient atmospheric pressure. Input air is either from static ports in the pitot tube, or from dedicated flush- mounted heated, static ports located on the side of the fuselage. The pressure is conveyed through a series of airtight tubes to the instruments that require the use of atmospheric pressure. This includes the air speed indicator, the variometer and the altimeter. On a modern more complex aircraft, the static system conveys ambient air pressure to a digital air data computer. In addition, the computer processes the ambient air pressure outputs for the auto-pilot system, the transponder, the flight management computers, IRS navigation units and more.

questions.question: What are the 14 CFR 43 and or 91 requirements for static system checks?
questions.idealAnswer: The aircraft must be inspected and tested for leaks after installation of any component parts, or when system malfunction is suspected. It must also be tested every 24 calendar months on an IFR certified aircraft intended to be flown as such. This is specified in 14 CFR 91.411. Licensed airframe and A&P technicians may perform this check. A test unit is used to check the system. It is attached to the static port end of the static system. Air pressure is then reduced by the test unit until it causes 1,000 feet to be indicated on the altimeter. This pressure is held for one minute. A reduction of altitude indication of more than 100 feet is not allowed. Systematic leak checking must be performed until the leak is located, repaired, and the system passes the check.

questions.question: Describe instrument range markings and their various markings.
questions.idealAnswer: Many instruments contain colored markings on the dial face to indicate, at a glance, whether a particular system or component is within range of operation that is safe and desirable or if undesirable conditions exist. These are put on the instrument by the original equipment manufacturer in accordance with the aircraft’s specifications in the Type Certificate Data Sheet. Occasionally the airframe technician may find it necessary to apply these markings. The marks can be in the form of a colored arch, or, as a radial line. Red is used to indicate maximum and minimum range values. Green indicates normal operating range. Yellow is used to indicate caution. Blue and white are used on airspeed indicators to define specific conditions.
